Automated Data Extraction
Take the Browser Copilot one step further by adding scraping capabilities.

How it works: Uses Beautiful Soup + Playwright to extract structured data.
Commands: "Go to Amazon, search for laptops under $1000, and save the top 10 results to a CSV on my desktop."

Ghost Cursor (Precision OS Control)
How it works: We divide your screen into a grid numerically (like a grid overlay). We use PyAutoGUI to give MARK absolute control over your physical mouse cursor.
Commands: "MARK, move mouse to the top right and click the volume icon." or "Scroll down fast."

Instant Local Dictation (Lightning Fast)
How it works: We integrate a tiny Whisper.cpp model entirely locally. When you hold a specific key combination (e.g., Command+Space), MARK instantly types whatever you say directly into whatever app you have open, much faster and more accurately than macOS's built-in dictation.

Spotlight-Style Floating Command Palette

What it is: You never have to open the MARK browser tab again. Hitting a hotkey (like Option + Space) summons a glassmorphic, floating search bar directly in the center of your Mac screen (built using PyQt6 or similar overlay tech).
Why it’s cool: Type a command silently and hit Enter. The bar vanishes instantly, and MARK executes the task in the background.

FastAPI / Asyncio Architecture Rewrite

What it is: We upgrade the core server from Flask (synchronous) to FastAPI (fully asynchronous).
Why it’s fast: Currently, if MARK is running a massive Universal Search, other background tasks might bottleneck. With asyncio, MARK can run web research, file searching, UI updates, and TTS audio generation concurrently at the exact same time without blocking.

Role & Goal:
Act as an expert Systems Programmer and OS Developer. Guide me through building a simple, 32-bit bare-metal operating system from scratch. We will use x86 Assembly, C, and the GRUB bootloader. The final output must be an .iso file that I can boot inside VirtualBox.

Please provide the code, terminal commands, and explanations for each of the following phases, one step at a time. Ask me if I am ready to proceed after completing each phase.

Phase 1: Environment & Toolchain Setup

Explain the necessity of a cross-compiler (e.g., i686-elf-gcc).

Provide the exact terminal commands to install the required dependencies (NASM, GCC, Make, GRUB, and xorriso) for my host operating system.

Guide me on setting up my project directory structure (e.g., /src, /boot, /linker).

Phase 2: The Bootloader (Assembly)

Write a simple Multiboot-compliant bootloader in x86 Assembly (boot.s).

Explain the Multiboot header magic numbers and what they do.

Set up the initial stack pointer and hand off control to the C kernel.

Phase 3: The Core Kernel (C)

Write a freestanding C program (kernel.c) that serves as the entry point.

Implement a simple VGA text mode driver to print "Hello, World! My OS is booting!" to the screen.

Explain how the VGA text buffer works at memory address 0xB8000.

Phase 4: Linking and Building

Provide the Linker Script (linker.ld) to map our kernel into memory at 1M (1 Megabyte).

Write a Makefile to automate compiling the Assembly file, compiling the C file, linking them together, and generating an .iso using grub-mkrescue.

Phase 5: VirtualBox Deployment

Provide the exact instructions on how to create a new virtual machine in VirtualBox configured for a 32-bit custom OS.

Explain how to mount the generated .iso and boot it.
